Driven by rapid prototyping and clean design, we excel at taking sophisticated tech concepts and transforming them into slick, highly engaging interactive products. We’re always excited to collaborate with visionaries, creative thinkers, and problem solvers who love pushing boundaries and making complex ideas effortlessly simple
summary:
Go-No-Go is a free browser game where players run a space agency and take a mission from idea to operations. They follow the real project lifecycle, from Pre-Phase A to Phase F.

Players negotiate requirements with stakeholders, design the orbit, and choose the satellite class. They then build the spacecraft from real NASA technologies, each with its actual TRL, mass, and power. Every choice changes the mass, power, DeltaV, data, and cost budgets (Z coins) and adds entries to a live risk register. Each phase ends with a review that gives a GO or a NO-GO. The satellite is then tested, launched, and flown in a Mission Control simulation, where the player watches their decisions succeed or fail. Zorty, our alien engineer, guides beginners, while a creative mode and consortia let players experiment and work together.

This way, the trade-offs that usually stay abstract in a classroom become choices players feel, with real consequences.

Often missions fail in meetings, budgets, and reviews long before they reach orbit, and few students ever practice that work. This way, more future engineers will be able to approach this process in a fun way.
The game will stay free for players and be funded by agencies and companies that want to show their technologies to future engineers.
details:
Go No-Go is an educational browser game that lets players experience the decisions behind a space mission, from the first idea to launch and operations.

Players run a space agency, negotiate mission objectives, select scientific instruments and spacecraft subsystems, assemble a CubeSat, and plan its orbit. They then work through engineering reviews and tests before making a GO/NO-GO launch decision. Every choice involves trade-offs: adding an instrument may improve scientific value, for example, but also increase the mission’s mass, power needs, and cost.

The game brings systems engineering to life through an interactive 3D campus, resource management and mission simulations. Tutorial and sandbox modes support different ways of learning. Players can also take part in joint missions, with up to four people sharing planning, satellite, science and communications roles and voting on whether to launch.

Go No-Go aims to make space mission design approachable for students and curious learners while showing why successful missions depend on cooperation, testing, and careful use of limited resources. Its component catalog includes technologies inspired by real NASA projects. The game provides immediate orbital estimates and can use NASA’s General Mission Analysis Tool (GMAT), when available, for more detailed analysis.

The project was developed with JavaScript, Three.js, Vite, Node.js, and PostgreSQL. It supports English and Italian and runs in a web browser. Its simulations and component values are educational approximations, rather than substitutes for professional mission engineering.
